name: Site diaries and daily reports
one_line: The serial, day-by-day record of a site kept while the work happens: who was on site and for how long, what plant stood idle, what the weather did, what was instructed verbally, what was delivered and what went wrong. Its defining property is that it is written to be READ LATER BY SOMEONE ELSE — a diary is the evidence base a delay claim, a variation, an accident investigation or an adjudication is built from, which is why it is kept daily rather than when something happens. The anchor is ONE SITE ON ONE DAY, and the corpus is a long run of near-identical documents whose value lies in the run being unbroken. Absorbs the legacy row cons.site-diary. Gist-level placeholder (J-IND): it recognises the situation and writes NO field rows, because the construction_property schema declares none.

deterministic: PRECONDITION: every entry below is a DETECTION signal and never an extraction licence. The construction_property schema declares no field rows (D1 as narrowed, _CONTRACT rules 10 and 15, CONNECTION PR-6), so nothing here writes a domain fact; detection exists so the material is recognised, kept where this row’s sensitivity says, and offered honestly. “Privacy policy must be enforced before content reaches any model or external connector.”

the diary form structure, which is the single most characteristic signal in this row: one page or one sheet per calendar day carrying labelled slots for date, weather (often with a morning and afternoon reading, or a temperature and a rainfall note), a labour return counted by trade, a plant-on-site list, visitors, deliveries received, instructions given, and a delays or events narrative box. No other document in this family pairs a weather slot with a labour count. “Tables matter because resumes, forms, applications, invoices, and administrative documents often place their most useful information in cells rather than body paragraphs.”
a labour allocation return: a table of operative names or trades against hours, repeated per day, with a total column — the diary's numeric half, frequently a separate sheet in the same workbook.

serial dating as the file's organising principle: a run of files or a run of worksheet tabs named for consecutive dates or week numbers, in which the individual member is unremarkable and the SEQUENCE is the artefact. A single isolated day-sheet is far weaker evidence than five in sequence.

a daily or weekly progress report addressed outward — to the client, the contract administrator or the employer's agent — carrying a period covered, a percentage or milestone progress statement, and a look-ahead section.
a confirmation-of-verbal-instruction note: a short dated memo recording something said on site, naming who said it, and stating that it is confirmed in writing because it was not issued formally.

an app export: a PDF or CSV generated by a site-diary or site-management application, recognisable by a machine-consistent layout repeated identically across every day, an auto-inserted weather line pulled from a forecast service, and photo thumbnails embedded in the day's page.
a delay or disruption record: a dated narrative of a stoppage naming a cause, a start and end time, the trades affected and the resources standing idle.
parent-folder context naming a site, a job number or a month, treated as a clue once one of the structures above is present. Folder context never fires alone.
needs_llm: PRECONDITION: a diary names individual workers, records their attendance and sometimes their conduct, and may narrate an injury, so any model step runs after P7 and under the user's policy. “Protected material should not be included in cloud-model prompts by default, should not display raw content in general group summaries, and should not be moved automatically without a user policy that explicitly permits it.”

the central determination for this row: separating a DIARY from a MEETING RECORD. Both are dated narratives of what was said and agreed on a site. The honest discriminant is the trigger — a diary is written because the day happened, a site-meeting minute is written because a meeting was convened, and it carries an attendee list, numbered action items and a next-meeting date.

an unlabelled day-sheet: a scanned handwritten A5 page with a date, some trade names and a weather word, and no form furniture at all. This is the commonest real diary and the hardest file in the row.

separating a diary entry that is merely a record from one written as CLAIM MATERIAL — the same page, in the same book, with the same handwriting, becomes the exhibit in a delay claim. “Topic answers what a file is about, while purpose answers what the file was for.”

a purpose-coherent claim bundle whose members are individually unremarkable — a run of diary pages, a weather report, a programme extract and two photographs, assembled for one argument. “The documents are content-incoherent but purpose-coherent.”
in every case above, abstention is the required outcome where the evidence does not settle it. “A model that cannot cite sufficient evidence must return unknown.”
never_alone: a date alone, or a run of dates alone. Serial dating is this row's strongest structural signal and its most dangerous one: expense logs, mileage sheets, medication charts, food diaries, delivery schedules and shift rotas all have exactly this shape.
a weather line alone. Weather appears in sailing logs, agricultural records, insurance claims and travel journals, and app-generated weather lines are auto-inserted rather than observed.

a UK-style postcode or a street address alone. An address is the single most tempting token in this whole family and it appears in every role at once — the site, the client’s home, the contractor’s registered office, the architect’s letterhead, a supplier’s depot, and a comparable property cited in a report. 00 states the same ambiguity for a university name: “A university name alone should not create a group because Columbia can appear as an authoring school, course provider, target institution, employer, research venue, or merely a cited organization.” — the address case is worse, and this is recorded as inference because 00 writes that sentence about a university, not an address.

a personal name alone, and this row is dense in them. An operative list is a list of people, and 00's corpus sentence names the category the moment it is: the corpus “can include identity documents, account statements, tax records, medical information, legal records, credentials, private correspondence, GPS metadata, employment materials, and educational records”.

the word 'diary', 'daybook', “log” or “journal” in a filename. A personal journal and a site diary are the same three words and radically different privacy postures, and getting this backwards is the worst outcome available in this row.
the presence of an embedded photograph. A diary page with a photo is not thereby a progress-photography record; the photo is the diary's attachment.

source_type or extension alone. “treat the file extension as a routing signal rather than an assumption about meaning”, and file_kind_plausible is constitutionally never-alone (CONNECTION section 5, invariant 2).
membership in a download session — a whole project folder or a document-portal export pulled down at once. “A session should never be treated as proof of topic”
a bare 4-digit number read as a year. It is at least as often a drawing number, a job number, a plot number, a house number, a cost code, or a British Standard reference.

a PDF author, producer, or company metadata string alone. “PDF metadata should be treated as supporting evidence, not as truth” — one contractor’s template stamps the same firm on every blank form it ever generated.

work_types: daily site diary page or day sheet
labour allocation sheet or labour return
weather record or weather report extract
daily or weekly progress report to the client
daily photograph log or diary photo appendix
grouping_reasons: one site across one period — the clearest group in this row, and the one users most expect: the run, not the page, is the artefact.
one month or one week of diary pages joined by nothing but consecutive dates, which is a real reason to group and the reason a date must never become an activation proof on its own.

one delay event: the diary pages that cover it, the weather report, the programme extract and the correspondence — purpose-coherent even where the members share no content. “The documents are content-incoherent but purpose-coherent.”
one diary re-exported over time from an app, joined by the universal duplicate_family and version_family facts rather than by any construction fact.
no group at all is a valid outcome: a single scanned day-sheet with no site named is an ordinary standalone record.
and the stop rules apply as written — “when members carry irreconcilable course, institution, project, term, or purpose facts” — two sites' diaries in one folder do not merge.

template.why: Empty by binding contract: a dimension may only branch on a field the same entry’s schema declares, and construction_property declares none (D1 as narrowed, _CONTRACT rules 10 and 15, CONNECTION PR-6). That is a contract fact, not a claim that this situation has no shape — it plainly does, and it is recorded here as PROSE for whoever answers the schema row’s open_question. The recommendation, held as prose: the site or project first, then the period (year then month, or week-commencing) as the second level, and the diary function last where a folder mixes diaries with progress reports and delay records. The site must come above the date because a bare date is meaningless across a contractor's whole corpus and actively harmful — every site has a 14 March — which is 00's own reason for putting a course above a homework number. This is the one row in this family where the second level is genuinely temporal: a diary IS a calendar object, and users look for it by date. That does not make the row time-first, because the top level must still be the site. 00’s own ordering reason applies: “a parent dimension should provide the context required to understand the child”. Not time-first — “For document and record domains, project, function, or subject usually comes before time because putting year first scatters related work across calendar folders.” at the top level, for the reason just given, even though its second level is a period. And whatever eventually lands stays a recommendation: “The system recommends an order based on the domain template, but the user can reverse, remove, add, or flatten dimensions.”

collides_with.signal: The load-bearing collision on this row. Both are dated narratives of what happened on a site and who said what. The discriminating evidence: an attendee list, numbered action items with owners, and a next-meeting date support the meeting row; a weather slot, a labour return, a plant list and one page per calendar day support this row. Provenance: inference.

A diary page written up as claim material and a confirmation of verbal instruction are simultaneously this row's serial record and that row's opening evidence. The discriminating evidence: a numbered variation or claim reference, a quantified time or money consequence, and an addressed notice support the claim row; an unaddressed daily entry in an unbroken run supports this row. Provenance: inference.

App-generated diaries embed photographs and photo packs carry dates, so the two rows meet on the same day's evidence. The discriminating evidence: camera EXIF with capture time on standalone image files supports the photography row — “Camera EXIF, GPS, and capture time can support deterministic photo-event proposals.” — while a document page with an embedded thumbnail supports this row. Provenance: inference.

Site attendance, induction records, permits issued and incident narratives are recorded in the diary and also kept as safety documents in their own right. The discriminating evidence: a hazard-and-control structure, a permit form, or an injury record supports the safety row; a general day narrative that merely mentions them supports this row. Where an injury is named, the safety row and its protective ordering win. Provenance: inference.

The same labour table read for pay rather than for the site, and the row that receives the coverage refused from construction_property.timesheet (see that row's refuse_reason). The discriminating evidence: pay rates, deductions, a tax reference or a payroll-period header support the hr row; a site or cost-code column, plant standing time and a weather line support this row. The hr reading is the more sensitive of the two and where both fire the stricter posture wins. Provenance: inference.

A daily-serial operational log with vehicles, hours and delays is the same shape in a haulage business. The discriminating evidence: a vehicle registration, a route or drop sequence and a driver's-hours reference support the logistics row; a fixed site, a trade-by-trade labour return and a weather slot support this row. Provenance: inference.

A daily production log and a site diary are both serial dated operational records with shift, headcount and downtime columns. The discriminating evidence: a batch, line, or work-order reference supports the manufacturing row; a site address, weather and trades support this row. Provenance: inference.

falls_through_to.why: The right home for a single day-sheet, a progress report or a confirmation of verbal instruction that arrives with no run of siblings around it — a durable record with no group. “Independent Records may live under Personal/Independent Records and hold standalone certificates, notices, confirmations, forms, and PDFs that have a durable purpose but no broader group.”

The honest outcome for the labour allocation sheet whose site and purpose are unresolved, and for a diary export whose members have not been read. “Review Later may hold files whose meaning is partly understood but whose final location requires a future decision.”

Diaries name individual workers and occasionally narrate an injury, and the personal-journal false positive lands here rather than in a work tree. This is also the home for any diary page carrying health information. “Protected Records may represent sensitive isolated material such as passport scans, medical documents, account statements, visas, legal forms, or credentials; it should normally remain local-only and must not cause filenames or content to be exposed in model prompts.”

The home for a photograph of a diary page with no OCR text and no run around it. “One-Off Images may live under Photos/One-Off Images and hold images with no event, project, reference collection, or photo-family association.”

Password-protected diary exports and proprietary site-app bundles are ordinary here. “Unsupported or Encrypted may hold—or, more safely, represent without moving—password-protected archives, unreadable documents, damaged files, and unknown formats.”

Delivery notes signed into the diary's delivery log, arriving alone, are transactional documents rather than diary pages. “Receipts and Confirmations may hold isolated invoices, delivery confirmations, booking records, boarding passes, purchase receipts, event tickets, and similar transactional documents.”

sensitivity_why: A diary is a daily attendance record of named individuals — who was present, for how long, who was late, who was sent home — and it periodically narrates an injury or a disciplinary event. 00's corpus sentence names both categories the moment it does: the corpus “can include identity documents, account statements, tax records, medical information, legal records, credentials, private correspondence, GPS metadata, employment materials, and educational records”. Beyond that, and as inference rather than a design claim, a diary is written to be evidence, so it is disproportionately likely to be read later by an adversary; that is a further reason for the cautious setting. This row assigns only the catalogue value potentially_sensitive; the handling class is P7's and is not set here.
open_question: Two. (1) Whether a personal journal and a site diary can be separated reliably enough at detection time to be safe. Their filenames are identical, their structure (dated entries) is identical, and only content settles it — which means the safe default for an unread file named like a diary is the protective home, not the construction row. This is the sharpest privacy question in the construction family and it is stated here rather than resolved. (2) Where the labour allocation sheet lands now that construction_property.timesheet is refused (see that row's refuse_reason). This row claims the site reading and routes the pay reading to hr.payroll-benefits-administration; R1c should confirm that split rather than inherit it.
